item.content:encoded:
Despite dour predictions from some insiders, Los Angeles Dodgers superstar Shohei Ohtani might be back in action for the Boys in Blue sooner rather than later.
Ohtani hit off a tee on Tuesday in his bid to return from knee, arm and neck pain, issues that led to a very uncharacteristic slump in the weeks before he was placed on the injured list.
Having already been shut down as a pitcher, Ohtani has also been sidelined as a hitter, though that may not be for too much longer.
Dave Roberts shares expectations for Ohtani’s return
On Tuesday, manager Dave Roberts said Ohtani “felt good” after hitting off the tee.
“I don’t know what’s in store for tomorrow, but I know there’s going to be a consistent buildup. Don’t know when the time of return to play is, but today was positive and hopefully, we can just keep building towards that,” he said.
When asked if he expects Ohtani back during the regular season, Roberts answered with a definitive “I do.”
View this post on Instagram
“Whether it happens or not is to be determined, but I do expect him to be back to play in some regular season games,” he said. “Don’t know how many though.”
Roberts’ prediction flies in the face of at least one Dodgers insider, who predicted that the Japanese superstar was out for the rest of 2026.
The saga has also raised questions about whether Ohtani was honest with the team about his injuries, and whether the team perhaps mismanaged their superstar.
Many of those questions will only be answered with time, though if Ohtani does indeed come back this year and looks more like his old self, the criticism will likely be much quieter.
What would Shohei Ohtani’s return mean for the Dodgers?
While Ohtani’s absence hasn’t impacted the Dodgers too much this month, that could be because the Boys in Blue have one of the easier September scheduled in the National League.
In October, though, the playoffs are on, and the quality of opponent will be much higher.
Some of those likely opponents, such as the Atlanta Braves, have recently given the Dodgers fits, and a healthier Ohtani returning to the batting order would almost assuredly improve the Dodgers’ chances of winning a third straight World Series.
Ohtani’s replacement, the much-hyped prospect Josue De Paula, has flashed moments of brilliance in his first few games in the big leagues, but getting back perhaps the best baseball player ever would be a huge boost for the Dodgers, especially from a mental perspective.
Do you think Shohei Ohtani will be back this year and, if so, will it be before the playoffs begin?

The Los Angeles Dodgers may have spoiled Josue De Paula's breakout game, but his monster home run against the Miami Marlins on Sunday sent a message: this kid may live up to his billing as LA's No. 1 prospect.
The Dodgers still have to figure out how they're going to fit him on the roster when Shohei Ohtani comes off the IL, but as long as his brief audition at the tail end of this season continues to go well, that should be a priority this offseason.
Maybe we're getting way ahead of ourselves here, but if the Dodgers figure out how to get him regular at-bats in 2027, we could be looking at the next in a long and storied line of Dodgers Rookie of the Year Award-winners.
The Dodgers have an MLB-leading 18, beginning, of course, with Jackie Robinson in 1947, the man the award is named after. Their latest winner was Cody Bellinger in 2017.
Sandwiched in between are franchise legends Jim Gilliam, Fernando Valenzuela, Eric Karros, and Hideo Nomo, just to name a few. De Paula could find himself in some very good company by the end of 2027.
Putting Josue De Paula's future Rookie of the Year campaign into context with other Dodgers greats
De Paula has been compared heavily to Yordan Alvarez, probably Andrew Friedman's greatest trade regret as the Dodgers' chief executive. Of the 12 position player Rookies of the Year the Dodgers have produced, none are quite the same archetype as Alvarez — David Ortiz, Kyle Schwarber-esque players who can flat-out hit.
But perhaps the most apt comparison is Mike Piazza, LA's winner in 1993. Piazza came into the league with far fewer expectations attached than De Paula, but both are defensively weaker position players with massive power potential and advanced plate discipline. De Paula has yet to strike out in the four games he's appeared in.
It would be unfair to expect the same kind of offensive production from De Paula that Piazza offered up in his rookie season, when he hit .318 with a .932 OPS, 35 homers, and 112 RBI to kick off what would become a Hall of Fame career.
But when the Dodgers, who are usually so enthused about their prospects, were all but champing at the bit to find him a place to play this season, that says a lot as to where they think his ceiling could be.

The Dodgers manager told reporters Tuesday night that Muncy, infielder Alex Freeland, and outfielder Josue De Paula weren't expected to start Wednesday, according to DodgerBlue on X.com.
The reasoning behind the move is that Andrew Abbott is scheduled to start for the Reds, a lefty with a 6-11 record and a 4.78 ERA this season. All three batters are left-handed hitters who have struggled against left-handed pitching.
We will probably have to remind everyone tomorrow, but Dave Roberts already said Max Muncy, Alex Freeland and Josue De Paula aren’t expected to be in the lineup.
— Dodger Blue (@DodgerBlue1958) September 16, 2026
Muncy has hit .222 against left-handed pitching over his career, compared to .235 against right-handers. Ironically, this season, Muncy has hit better against pitching from the left side, batting .257 with six home runs and 15 RBIs versus .249 with 22 homers and 56 RBIs against the right side.
Those numbers have shaped how Roberts has deployed Muncy late in games and against certain matchups. The 36-year-old is in the middle of a bounce-back year that included his third career All-Star selection, his first since 2021.
The Dodgers enter Wednesday's game with a 92-59 record and a 10-game lead over the San Diego Padres in the National League West, needing just one more win or a Padres loss to clinch the division. The Dodgers have already locked up a playoff berth for the 14th straight season, tying the major league record with the Atlanta Braves.
While the Dodgers will be without left-handed bats, Roberts will lean on left-hander Blake Snell on the mound, giving the Dodgers the best possible matchup to attack Abbott without their top left-handed bats.

The Los Angeles Dodgers designated outfielder Ryan Ward for assignment ahead of Wednesday’s game, ending his seven-year stay in the Dodgers’ organization.
To replace Ward on the 40-man roster, the Dodgers reinstated trade deadline acquisition Kris Bubic from the 60-day injured list while optioning right-hander Paul Gervase to Triple-A.
Ward, 28, made his MLB debut with the Dodgers this season, but his time in the organization goes well beyond the 20 games he played for the team this season.
He begun making headlines during the 2025 season for his unbelievable performances in Triple-A, with many calling for him to replace outfielder Michael Conforto, who struggled during his one-year tenure in Los Angeles.
Ward won the Pacific Coast League MVP in 2025, hitting 36 homers and driving in 122 runs over the course of 143 games, posting a career-high .937 OPS. He hadn’t appeared in MLB since June prior to his DFA.
Why Did the Dodgers Choose to DFA Ward Over a Pitcher?
While the Dodgers have plenty of pitchers on their 40-man roster, especially some who haven’t performed up to MLB standards this season, so why DFA Ward?
The decision likely comes due to Ward’s positional redundancy. A left-handed outfielder, which the Dodgers have plenty of—especially after calling up Josue De Paula directly from Double-A last week.
The Dodgers view De Paula as the future and already have him in MLB, which effectively put the nail in the coffin for Ward’s time with the Dodgers.
De Paula, the Dodgers’ top prospect, only has five MLB games under his belt, but is turning heads across the league already. He has a homer and three RBIs to go with five walks and a .797 OPS across his five appearances.
How Did Ryan Ward Perform in the Majors?
Ward had a decent year in the majors for the Dodgers, but not quite up to his standards in Triple-A. Through his 20 games, he stepped up to the plate 60 times and posted a .738 OPS.
He hit three homers over the course of those games, driving in 12 runs, though his OPS sat below .300 for all of the final 12 games with the Dodgers.
The 28-year-old got off to a good start with the Dodgers when they called him up for two games in April, logging two hits in his debut and driving in his first MLB RBI.
He came back at the end of May, hitting his first career home run against the Philadelphia Phillies, the. crushed another one against the Los Angeles Angels a few days later. Ward rode a five-game hit streak from June 4-10, but struggled to put up results for the remainder of the year. He logged just four hits over the following 11 games.
Ward returned to the minors at the end of June and had a decent couple of months, but a September slump may have cost him his spot on the 40-man roster. Since Sept. 1, Ward had a .191 batting average with a .565 OPS, hitting just one home run in a hitter-friendly league.
LA can still keep Ward if he clears waivers, but the probability of teams passing on a player with his track record is extremely low.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to win their series against the Cincinnati Reds on Wednesday.
The Dodgers took Monday's series opener, 4-1, behind seven shutout innings from Tarik Skubal. Then, they won Tuesday's game, 4-0, behind seven shutout innings from Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
On Wednesday, LA has another superstar pitcher on the mound in left-hander Blake Snell.
“When you’re writing in the lineup and you see those guys, and one trying to up the other guy, and then now you got Snell going [Wednesday] — you feel good about preventing runs,” manager Dave Roberts said.
“A team like the Reds right now, where they’re scuffling a little bit, it’s daunting when you see a starter like those guys that we’re running out there.”
Dodgers vs Reds Pitching Matchup on Wednesday
Snell is looking to continue his run of dominance since returning from midseason elbow surgery.
The left-hander has gone 4-0 with a 1.04 ERA across six starts, striking out 46 while allowing zero home runs over 34.2 innings of work.
Snell, who pitched 5.2 innings in his most recent start, is still looking to go deeper into games moving forward. He hasn't pitched more than six innings in any of his six starts.
“I mean the goal, at worst is definitely six for me,” Snell said. “I also know that I can go seven, eight, nine. I know I’m able to do it. So for me not to, I just have to get more efficient early in the game. I feel like once I get past the first couple innings, I start cruising and start figuring it out."
Opposite Snell will be left-hander Andrew Abbott, who's 6-11 with a 4.78 ERA and 120 strikeouts over 154.1 innings this season.
He's allowed seven earned runs in two of his last three starts, and has a 7.71 ERA since the start of August.

Josue De Paula received a huge shoutout from one of baseball's biggest stars.
Juan Soto posted a clip of De Paula on his Instagram story, where the Dodgers top prospect was in the midst of working his fifth walk in just four major league games. The New York Mets star called De Paula "el loco mio" on his story as MLB compared the 21-year-old's stance to Soto's.
De Paula and Soto both attended "El Niche" baseball academy in the Dominican Republic. Soto, who had a chance to sign with the Dodgers ahead of the 2025 season, has evidently not lost love for his fellow countryman and budding star.
As for whether De Paula was trying to copy the Soto Shuffle, the Dodgers outfielder explained what was going through his head during that at-bat.
"I wasn't exactly trying to emulate it. It was more just me being so locked in and getting into my legs," he told the California Post Tuesday. "But I can understand how it looks like a Soto shuffle. And if people think it looks like that, hey, I'm not mad at it."
De Paula and Soto have developed a relationship as the pair share representation with Boras Coporation. It appears the former has begun his own version of the Soto Shuffle.
The Dodgers promoted De Paula from Double-A last week to fill in for the injured Shohei Ohtani. Despite being the youngest player in the lineup, De Paula exudes confidence and power when he steps in the batter's box.
Moreover, the De Paula's plate discipline is a rarity for young players. Yet, entering Tuesday night's game he had managed to avoid striking out.
Who else does that remind you of?
Soto.

item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman has been battling right knee pain, but the worst of it may be behind the team’s contact specialist.
Entering Tuesday’s game, Freeman was on a 3-for-30 cold streak and had missed three of the last six games because of his knee issue.
Things looked shaky for Freeman, who has built a reputation as one of baseball’s most consistent players.
However, he put together his best game in weeks, going 3-for-5 on singles, but showing the elite bat-to-ball skills that make him a candidate to bat around .300 year in, year out.
After the game, manager Dave Roberts noted that Freeman looked more like himself.
“It looked good,” Roberts said. “It looked more like Freddie.”
Freeman had asked Roberts before the game, jokingly, if he could play on Wednesday, a scheduled day off, if he got three hits.
As a result of Freeman’s performance, the manager is allowing Freeman to skip an off-day on Wednesday and play again, with the infielder eager to get the ball rolling.
“I feel like my faults are I try to hit the ball to the opposite field too much, and I let the ball get too deep,” he said.
“So today was [get the] foot down early, catch the ball out front a little bit, and it kind of worked. I wasn’t squaring the ball up in the game, but I’ll take those three hits and keep that work going tomorrow, and hopefully we’ll get hot.”
What does Freeman’s uptick mean for the Dodgers?
With the best rotation in baseball, the Dodgers are left scrounging around for offense any way that they can find it.
Teoscar Hernandez, Josue De Paula, and Mookie Betts have been the most consistent sources, with Max Muncy and Will Smith in the picture as well.
Still, the Dodgers need as many players in a spot as possible to deliver timely hits, and Freeman’s experience and skills make him a clear-cut candidate to step up.
To deliver results quickly, as he manages his knee and struggles, Freeman has made a mechanical change, getting out in front of the ball to catch it earlier on his bat.
The result may be less clean contact and hard hits, but more consistent contact, with the idea that it makes him valuable come the postseason.
“I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable,” he said. “I’m trying to find something that works for four weeks.”
Freeman has the right approach to deliver just what the Dodgers need. The entire offense does not need to be excellent; simply being good enough will lead to a three-peat.

When the Los Angeles Dodgers promoted Josue De Paula to the majors last week, they did so in full knowledge that the 21-year-old had more errors (eight) than assists (six) as a Double-A outfielder.
After playing 58 games in left field and 37 in right field for the Tulsa Drillers, De Paula has spent all but five innings at designated hitter during his first five days in the majors. When he caught the only fly ball hit in his direction over five innings Sunday in Miami, De Paula and the Dodgers could exhale. He got the first one out of the way.
It will be difficult for manager Dave Roberts to take De Paula out of the lineup once Shohei Ohtani returns from the injured list if he continues to reach base at such a high clip.
Yet it will be easier to keep De Paula in the lineup if he can play a corner outfield position. To that end, Roberts is hopeful the rookie can become a better defensive outfielder in short order.
"I just think that — just being candid — I don’t think that he’s valued it as much as he will," Roberts said, via Bill Plunkett of the Orange County Register. "And it just has to be important. Certainly, when you get to the big leagues, outs are important, converting outs are important.
“I think that he’s a young player. I mean, he’s 21 years old. His bat has certainly got him here, but it’s our job to make him value defense and get him to be a better defender.”
Besides their mandate to make De Paula a more complete baseball player, the Dodgers have another pressing reason to get the rookie comfortable in the outfield.
If Ohtani and Dalton Rushing are able to return from the injured list prior to October, they can only occupy the roster as designated hitters or pinch hitters. That's a limiting factor in the postseason, when teams can only carry 26 active players in each round.
De Paula gives the Dodgers three left-handed hitting DHs — impractical at best, impossible at worst — unless he can play the outfield.
"He and Dino [Ebel, the Dodgers' outfielders coach] are committed to a routine, which I love,” Roberts said. “I think the other important thing is just so he can see how the quality and how intense the work is up here. And I think that you really don’t know until you know, and I’m excited for him to watch our guys, how they prepare each night.”

CINCINNATI — Josue De Paula is in his element in the batter’s box. He carries himself like a guy who knows his importance to the Los Angeles Dodgers depends on how well he can command himself within those 24 square feet of chalk lines. De Paula asserts himself with a confident shake of the head after each pitch outside the strike zone.
Advertisement
Some head shakes are more exaggerated than others. Each demonstrates the same message: De Paula is not going to give in.
“I just want to feel saucy when I’m up there, you know what I’m saying?” De Paula told The Athletic this week. “I feel like I’m in control, not you. … I want my pitch. Come in the zone. Let’s go.”
This is who De Paula wants to be. He describes hitting as “aggressive patience,” an approach that puts him on the attack.
“It’s almost like a war for me in my head,” De Paula said. “I look confident. I look saucy. I feel saucy when I’m in the box, so it’s like, ‘Hey bro, let’s keep it rocking.’”
It took four games for De Paula to inspire fascination within the Dodgers dynasty, where his every at-bat feels like a must-watch example of how to command a zone. Of the first 37 big-league pitches De Paula saw outside of the strike zone, he swung at just five. He made it 17 plate appearances without striking out before going down swinging in the seventh inning and looking in the ninth in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win over the Reds on Tuesday. De Paula does not seem fazed that he is just 2 for 14 (.143) since being called up, including five hitless at-bats in his first game in the leadoff spot.
That’s because he believes in his process. A day earlier, De Paula battled back from down in the count against Reds lefty Nick Lodolo, a former All-Star. The left-handed batter took a 2-2 fastball just below the knees, crouched and shook his head. A pitch later, De Paula walked for the fifth time in his short career.
The clip of the head shake drew a chuckle from the proprietor of the “Soto Shuffle” himself, Juan Soto, who, like De Paula, once honed his craft at the El Niche Baseball Academy in the Dominican city of Santo Domingo.
Josue De Paula live reaction to you trying to get him to chase. https://t.co/CrmRSnDVgO pic.twitter.com/dbXGz8WYL0
— Chad Moriyama (@ChadMoriyama) September 14, 2026
“El loco mío,” Soto shared to his Instagram story in Spanish, stamping his approval with a laughing emoji. My guy.
Advertisement
“I swear I wasn’t trying to do like the whole thing,” De Paula said with a laugh. “I just got into my legs, and I was shaking my head … but I’m not mad. That’s not a bad player to look like.”
De Paula, 21, feels like an injection of youthful exuberance for baseball’s oldest lineup. The Brooklyn-born son of a Dominican father (and relative of NBA veterans Stephon Marbury and Sebastian Telfair) speaks with a thick New York accent and oozes the confidence of a player who carries that swagger into the box.
De Paula is the crown jewel of a Dodgers farm system that is expected to prolong this run of excellence. Last week, he became the first position player ever to be called up directly from Double A by this Andrew Friedman-led front office group.
De Paula is here because he can hit, has always hit, and the Dodgers need him to hit. De Paula is here to serve as the Dodgers’ designated hitter, at least until Shohei Ohtani returns from the injured list. No one with the Dodgers, however, is ruling out the possibility that De Paula could help them in October as they seek a third consecutive World Series title.
“I hope he makes our decision hard,” manager Dave Roberts said.
Through De Paula’s torrid run through the Dodgers’ farm system, officials raved about his keen ability to pick up the baseball, make proper swing decisions and recognize spin.
“He doesn’t give away any pitches, which I love, let alone give away any at-bats,” Roberts said.
Pair that with a preternatural ability to make contact, and De Paula entered this season as one of the highly-regarded young hitters in the league. The Dodgers implemented a change to De Paula’s swing this year, lowering his hands and opening up his resulting bat path to keep the barrel in the zone longer. That has allowed him to access more power by pulling more fly balls and has made him a lethal producer at Double A.
Advertisement
De Paula slugged 27 home runs this season in Double A, more than double what he had in any of his first four professional seasons. His first hit Sunday in Miami was a mammoth upper-deck shot to right field on the kind of awe-inspiring swing that has come much more easily for De Paula than in years past.
“When all those things are kind of clicking, it’s tough for any pitcher to compete with,” hitting coach Robert Van Scoyoc said. “So it’s been very impressive so far.”
De Paula became a Dodger partially as a byproduct of the COVID-19 pandemic, which shut down the New York baseball season and prompted De Paula’s father, Josue Sr., to send him to the Dominican Republic to work at El Niche under Cristian “Niche” Batista.
“It was like stepping into a whole other world,” De Paula said.
It was there, during an offseason workout, that De Paula met Soto, who broke into the big leagues at 19 years old with the kind of swaggering command of the batter’s box that De Paula hopes to replicate. Rather than enter the amateur draft, De Paula signed directly with the Dodgers as an international amateur for a bonus of just under $400,000. De Paula estimated that, in one of his two tryouts with the organization and with several of the club’s brass in attendance, he collected nine hits in 10 at-bats.
“I killed,” De Paula said, reliving the memory as if it just happened.
He has hit ever since, ascending to the top of prospect lists. His list of star-studded admirers grew, too. After accompanying Soto in being represented by super agent Scott Boras, De Paula was asked by Boras to name some of his favorite players. De Paula selected Elly De La Cruz, who at that time was set for his first season as a breakout star for the Cincinnati Reds but was already dominating the minor leagues. Boras invited De Paula to his Newport Beach offices in Southern California after that and surprised him by bringing De La Cruz.

The two have remained close, working out together in the Miami area in the winters. Friday, just before he made his major-league debut against the Marlins in Miami, De Paula called De La Cruz on FaceTime. When they met up again this week in Cincinnati, they posed for a picture.
“I’m really happy for what he’s doing,” De La Cruz said.
De Paula sees a kinship between De La Cruz and Soto.
“We’re all killers,” De Paula said with a knowing smirk.
When De Paula spent his first spring training in big-league camp with the Dodgers in 2025, he quickly heard from Mookie Betts. The former Gold Glove right fielder wanted to make De Paula and fellow newcomers Zyhir Hope and Justin Dean feel welcome, so over dinner at a Phoenix-area soul food restaurant, he talked shop. When De Paula went out for early defensive work in the outfield this week, he had Roberts and Betts at different points offer some advice.
Now in a clubhouse filled with stars, De Paula said he feels at home. Whether he stays there heading into October will depend on how the rest of the regular season goes. The first few games have left a strong first impression.
“It’s a slow heartbeat,” Van Scoyoc said. “He’s not overwhelmed at all. It seemed like he picked up where he left off in Double A. … I wouldn’t say it’s surprising, but it’s just nice to see.”
Ohtani is expected to return from his nagging biceps and knee injuries by year’s end. De Paula has a lack of defensive utility at this point. While he did play in left field on Sunday, the Dodgers still want to work on getting De Paula to “value” the defensive side of the ball first, Roberts said. That means his path to the Dodgers’ postseason roster will likely be as a left-handed bat off the bench, essentially the role the club envisioned for Dalton Rushing before his most recent IL stint.

That decision is still up in the air, Roberts said. There will be “growing pains,” as Roberts said after Tuesday’s performance. The manager said he “didn’t love” the quality of De Paula’s at-bats. But October is a scenario De Paula feels he will be ready for.
“Especially in big moments, I feel like my mind just goes to a whole ‘nother level,” De Paula said. “Especially competing. The bigger the moment is … it’s like the more my mind hyper-focuses. So when I’m hyper-focused like that a lot, it’s dangerous.”

The Dodgers’ winning ways in September were briefly interrupted for two games against the Miami Marlins, but they have picked back up against the Cincinnati Reds, taking the first two games of a four-game set.
After Tarik Skubal shut down Cincinnati over seven innings on Monday, Yoshinobu Yamamoto continued the trend of marvelous results from the rotation with a seven-inning scoreless gem on Tuesday, working through a pair of lead-off walks while allowing just one hit while striking out seven. Yamamoto has amazed in his two most recent starts— both against the Reds— allowing just one run over 14 innings while racking up 17 strikeouts compared to just three walks.
Yamamoto held the Reds to just a 1-21 clip after walking his first two hitters of the game on Tuesday, and the right-hander managed to take a page out of Skubal’s playbook for his dominating efforts, notes Sonja Chen of MLB.com.
Yamamoto was able to learn from how the Reds approached Skubal the night before, and Snell was no doubt gathering similar information on Tuesday.
“That kind of encouraged me to be aggressive and attack the hitters,” Yamamoto said through interpreter Yoshihiro Sonoda.
The pitching has managed to hold their end of the bargain against Cincinnati this week, and Blake Snell looks to keep that trajectory in motion. On the offensive side of the ball, Teoscar Hernández has fortified the offense at Great American Ball Park, as the right-hander has crushed a pair of two-run home runs that put both games out of reach.
Hernández has once again found his stride that fans saw during spring training this year, and the Dodger outfielder’s recent success is the brainchild of hitting coach Aaron Bates, allowing Hernández to have a “twister tap” in his stride to the ball, per Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times.
“It was a great meeting we had,” Bates said. “We all talked about it, and then he felt comfortable enough to do it, and then the rest is to his credit. He’s just been who he is.”
“When Teo’s hips are loose that way, and his front leg looks like an Elvis knee, it’s a good sign for us,” Bates said. “Because that means that he can open and close it without his upper body going with it.”
Update on Shohei Ohtani
It’s an unusual feeling watching the Dodgers without Shohei Ohtani in the everyday lineup. So far, rookie Josue De Paula has filled in at DH to a small degree of success in limited time (.143/.368/.429, 19 PA) while the reigning two-time NL MVP recovers from multiple nagging issues.
Jack Harris of the California Post notes that Ohtani was able to take batting practice on Monday, and the team is optimistic that he can potentially return from the injured list before the end of the regular season.
“Today was positive,” Roberts said, “and hopefully we can just keep building towards that.”

CINCINNATI — Yoshinobu Yamamoto allowed one hit through seven innings as the Los Angeles Dodgers beat the Cincinnati Reds 4-0 on Tuesday night to edge closer to an NL West division title.
The Dodgers reduced the magic number to clinch their 13th division title in the past 14 seasons to two. Los Angeles wrapped up a playoff spot on Monday and still is vying for the top seed in the NL.
Cincinnati is assured of a non-winning season after its 81st loss.
Yamamoto (14-8) made his team-high 27th start and allowed only a third-inning double to Elly De La Cruz, after which he retired 10 straight. He walked two and struck out seven. It was the second straight game a Dodgers starter went seven scoreless after Tarik Skubal on Monday.
Dodgers pitching recorded its 12th shutout of the season. The Reds were blanked for the 17th time.
Freddie Freeman returned to the Dodgers lineup after missing three of the past five games with right knee soreness and had three singles in five at-bats. Freeman was 3 for 30 coming into Tuesday.
Josue De Paula batted leadoff for the first time in just his fifth career game for the Dodgers and went 0 for 5 with a strikeout. He's 2 for 14 since his callup.
Teoscar Hernandez's 15th homer of the season off right-hander Rhett Lowder followed a walk to Kyle Tucker and made the score 3-0 in the third. Lowder (6-11) allowed three earned runs on five hits in five innings.
Alex Freeland made the score 4-0 in the seventh with a solo homer off Pierce Johnson.
De La Cruz extended his on-base streak to 22 games dating to Aug. 22, going 2 for 3 with a double, walk, and stolen base.
Cincinnati had runners on first and third in the ninth against Tanner Scott who struck out the next three batters to seal the Dodgers' ninth straight win over the Reds.
Dodgers LHP Blake Snell (4-1, 1.91) will oppose Reds LHP Andrew Abbott (6-11, 4.84) on Wednesday.

How Teoscar Hernández fixed his swing to help power Dodgers over the Reds
- Click here to listen to this article
-
CINCINNATI — A simple change opened a dramatic offensive turnaround for Dodgers left fielder Teoscar Hernández.
Hernández’s two-run homer Tuesday, in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win against the Reds, was his second home run in as many nights, as the team trimmed its magic number to clinch the division to one behind Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s seven innings of one-hit ball. And, significantly, this one was against a right-handed pitcher.
“It’s been very helpful,” manager Dave Roberts said after the game. “As certain guys are not seeing the ball as well, it’s nice to kind of backfill with guys like Teo swinging the bat. And when you can slug like he can, you can win baseball games, and he can carry us for a while. And the last 10 days, something like that, it’s been really good from him.”
Through the end of August, Hernández had just a .668 OPS against right-handed pitchers this season. So, when Roberts was asked in Detroit whether the Dodgers would consider setting up a left-field platoon with the team’s September call-ups, he said yes.
Hernández homered off Tigers left-hander Framber Valdez on the last day of the series. And before the Dodgers opened a three-game set against the Cardinals at Dodger Stadium, Hernández met with the hitting coaches.
Against Valdez, Hernández was in a closed stance, to delay his front hip from opening, according to Dodgers hitting coach Aaron Bates. But the team’s hitting group thought a return to a familiar setup could be a long-term solution.
“It was a great meeting we had,” Bates said. “We all talked about it, and then he felt comfortable enough to do it, and then the rest is to his credit. He’s just been who he is.”
Edwin Díaz struggled in his rehab start Sunday, and Dave Roberts is making it clear the Dodgers “got to see something” before putting him on the playoff roster.
In the past, Hernández had used a “twister tap” as his stride. He started in a more open stance, tapped his toe in line with the pitcher, and then set his foot down. But lower-body injuries the last couple of years — a left groin strain last season and a left hamstring strain earlier this season — forced him away from it.
His improved health and hip flexibility opened the avenue for him to return to that timing mechanism.
“When Teo’s hips are loose that way, and his front leg looks like an Elvis knee, it’s a good sign for us,” Bates said. “Because that means that he can open and close it without his upper body going with it.”
The advantage of the twister tap, as Hernández explained it, is how repeatable it is. A more traditional stride can be sped up or slowed down.
“Just being able to control my body and being in a good position,” Hernández said earlier this month. “I can see the pitch a little sooner and identify what kind of pitch it is and if it’s going to be a strike or a ball.”
With that change, he’s rewarded the Dodgers for deciding against platooning left field. Hernández entered Tuesday with a .777 OPS against right-handed pitchers — a sample size of just 28 plate appearances but still a significant jump.
“The biggest thing is his plate coverage away,” Bates said. “Because now he can spoil pitches, and he’s staying in at-bats longer.”
Hernández’s dramatic offensive turnaround, along with fellow corner outfielder Kyle Tucker’s improvement, have helped steady a Dodgers offense that’s missing Shohei Ohtani (on the IL with right biceps and left knee injuries) and includes a hobbled Freddie Freeman (right knee soreness).
Rookie Josue De Paula, mostly filling in for Ohtani at designated hitter, has already shown he can take mature at-bats and provide some pop. But he’s still finding his footing in a new league.
It lengthens the Dodgers lineup for Hernández, after a slow start to his year, to return to being a veteran power threat — just in time to, ideally, carry the momentum into the postseason.
On Monday, he launched his two-run shot off left-hander Nick Lodolo. On Tuesday, he replicated the feat off right-hander Rhett Lowder.
On the second pitch of the at-bat, Hernández recognized a hung slider, and he roped it over the left-field fence at 109.3 mph, according to Statcast. The blast put the Dodgers up 3-0 in the third inning, with Dodgers starter Yamamoto settling into a groove on the other side.
Yamamoto had walked the first two batters he faced, but he reined in his control to pitch seven scoreless innings and allow just one more baserunner — a double by Reds star shortstop Elly De La Cruz.
The Dodgers also scored on Hunter Feduccia’s second-inning single and Alex Freeland’s seventh-inning homer. And the Dodgers bullpen completed the shutout.
Freeman staying in the lineup
Freeman was all smiles after his three-hit game Tuesday — after going hitless for his last four games.
“I was supposed to be off tomorrow, but I played myself in there,” he said. “So I’m very excited.”
Roberts explained: “He was joking, saying, ‘If I get three hits, then can I be in there tomorrow?’”
Sure enough, the mechanical adjustments he made in the batting cage — focusing on getting his foot down early and making contact out in front — got him there.
“I’m just trying to find something that gives me results,” Freeman said. “We’re at the time where we’re just trying to get hot for five weeks here. So kind of like I did in the World Series a couple years ago, I did the step-out move. That’s not sustainable over six months. I’m not trying to find something that’s sustainable.”
Though Roberts has been trying to find opportunities to rest Freeman, he saw promising signs Tuesday beyond the results.
“Just my eyes, just watching him move, I feel good about him going tomorrow,” Roberts said.
De Paula, Freeland and third baseman Max Muncy will be out of the lineup Wednesday, Roberts said.

With a spot in the MLB playoff locked up, the Los Angeles Dodgers have one major goal for the rest of September: get healthy.
Sure, there are sub-storylines to follow, from Josue De Paula filling in at DH, which bullpen arms are getting hot at the right time, and Kyle Tucker figuring it out down the stretch, but for the most part, the Dodgers simply want to take the field in October with their best guys all available for Dave Roberts to call upon.
Fortunately, on Tuesday, Roberts provided fans with some positive updates on that very front, noting that Shohei Ohtani and Andy Pages are trending in the right direction, as reported by The Athletic's Fabian Ardaya.

"Some more from Dave Roberts: Shohei Ohtani hit in the cage today. Hope is still for him to return before the end of the regular season," Ardaya wrote. "Andy Pages hit off the machine today. Plan is for him to do Trajekt next. Bullpen game on Thursday."
After breaking his hand in mid-August in a game against the Pittsburgh Pirates, Pages has missed almost a month as he works back from surgery. And as for Ohtani? Well, after missing four games earlier in the month, he returned for one but didn't ultimately look right, landing on the IL to allow him to recover from a series of injuries that have hampered his production down the stretch.
Without Pages and Ohtani, the Dodgers still found a way to manufacture offense, ripping off their longest win streak of the season, but folding that duo back into the fray, especially with De Paula proving he deserves a spot on the bench as a power-hitting pinch hitter, makes LA all the more dangerous down the stretch.

Kyle Tucker's home run Monday in Cincinnati was his third in his last five games. In that span he's raised his slugging percentage from a season-low .350 on Sept. 8 to .376 entering Tuesday's rematch against the Reds.
September is halfway through, and it's shaping into Tucker's best month of the season. If it seems like he's stopped pressing at the plate, perhaps Tucker let up on himself after getting some needed reassurance in a one-on-one meeting with Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts.
“I told him, I’m gonna ride or die with him,” Roberts said (via Jack Harris of the California Post). “That was my young term phrase.”
It's been a rough ride for Tucker in his first season in Los Angeles. The Dodgers signed the four-time All-Star to a four-year, $240 million contract over the winter. Despite being baseball's highest-paid player this season, Tucker hit only one home run in his first 17 games of the season.
Things didn't get much better from there. Among 138 qualified hitters through the end of August, Tucker's .683 OPS ranked 116th.
"I was prepared, the organization was prepared, to give him as much leash as we possibly could to work through some things, and I do think that now we’re starting to see the fruits,” Roberts said. “So I see no other reason why we would pivot from running him out there every day.”
Fans might beg to differ.
At Triple-A Oklahoma City, outfielder James Tibbs III has 29 home runs and 101 RBIs to go with a .417 on-base percentage. Prospect Josue De Paula, who's played right field in the minors, was promoted to take Shohei Ohtani's place on the active roster.
Since his debut, the 21-year-old has reached base in half of his first 14 plate appearances. Sunday, he hit his first career home run. Perhaps Roberts needed to reassure Tucker that De Paula wasn't coming for his job to unlock his production, a curious case of reverse psychology.
It will be hard for the Dodgers to take De Paula out of the lineup if he maintains his current level of production. Roberts said prior to Ohtani's IL stint that the team wasn't considering using him in the outfield.
Tucker, for his part, can reduce the Dodgers' temptation to use Ohtani or De Paula in right field if he continues to hit like a $60 million All-Star.

Josue De Paula earned comparisons throughout his Minor League career to some of MLB’s best players, whether for his overall offensive profile to Yordan Alvarez or his plate approach to Juan Soto. That’s why he’s been ranked as one of the sport’s best hitting prospects, making his big league debut last week as MLB Pipeline’s No. 6 prospect overall.
During Monday’s 4-1 Dodgers win over the Reds, De Paula put that Soto-like plate approach on full display. He drew a fifth-inning walk against Cincinnati starter Nick Lodolo after battling back from a 1-2 count.
The fifth pitch of the plate appearance fell just below the zone for ball three, prompting a challenge from Reds catcher Tyler Stephenson, who has been a top-10 challenging catcher this season based on Statcast’s Overturns vs. Expected metric. But Stephenson was wrong this time. Lodolo’s offering missed by 0.9 inches, according to the ABS Challenge System powered by T-Mobile.
De Paula seemed to know all along.
The 21-year-old rookie squatted in his stance, shaking his head in a display of confidence that was reminiscent of the famous “Soto Shuffle.” De Paula then watched a sinker finish well outside to earn the walk -- already his fifth in just four Major League games.
Even if you have to squint a bit to see the Soto Shuffle in De Paula’s reaction Monday night, it doesn’t take much effort to see why there are such widespread comparisons between De Paula and the Mets superstar.
Soto remains one of MLB’s best eyes at the plate at age 27, with a 98th-percentile walk rate (16.5%) and a 95th-percentile chase rate (20.7%) this season. As a 19-year-old rookie in 2018, Soto posted similarly elite numbers in walk rate (16%) and chase rate (18.4%).
De Paula, in his extremely limited Major League sample, has walked 35.7% of the time and chased just 13.5% of the time. Those numbers will balance out over time, but it’s still quite a start for the youngster.
De Paula’s connection with Soto goes back even further. A native of Brooklyn before he moved to the Dominican Republic in high school, De Paula trained at El Niche Baseball Academy, the same facility that worked with the likes of Soto, Elly De La Cruz and Otto Lopez. De Paula has also trained alongside Soto in the past.
In a playful moment between mentor and mentee, Soto shared De Paula’s charismatic take from Monday on his Instagram story, referring to De Paula as "el loco mio" ("my crazy guy" in Spanish).

Shohei Ohtani se ha perdido seis de los últimos siete partidos de Los Angeles Dodgers debido a las lesiones que ha venido arrastrando esta temporada. La primera fue en la rodilla, una molestia que lo alejó del montículo desde principios de julio y que, con poco tiempo para recuperarse antes de los playoffs, hace casi un hecho que no vuelva a lanzar en 2026. Una baja sensible para los Dodgers en el tramo más importante de la campaña, en el que buscan conquistar su tercera Serie Mundial consecutiva.
Shohei Ohtani to be placed on the injured list (left knee, right biceps), Dodgers manager Dave Roberts announces. pic.twitter.com/AG3VlX3TVe
— MLB (@MLB) September 10, 2026
La segunda lesión que sufrió esta temporada fue en el bíceps, una molestia que ha ido empeorando con el paso de las semanas. Ohtani comenzó a sufrir molestias en el cuello como consecuencia de este problema, lo que obligó a los Dodgers a colocarlo en la lista de lesionados y provocó que se perdiera los últimos encuentros. La buena noticia es que el japonés ha estado trabajando para regresar en este cierre de temporada regular y volver a ocupar su puesto como bateador designado de cara a los playoffs de la MLB.
Ohtani será fundamental en las aspiraciones de los Dodgers
Previo al inicio de la serie ante los Reds en Cincinnati, el mánager de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, confirmó que Ohtani tiene programado realizar swings desde un tee antes del partido del martes. La actividad representa un paso adelante en su recuperación y mantiene abierta la posibilidad de que pueda regresar a tiempo para ayudar a Los Angeles en los playoffs.
"I think it's important that he does pitch because he has the ability to do it. He's elite."@spillygoat19 shares his thoughts on whether or not he would discourage Shohei Ohtani from pitching in the future.
MLB Network + @NewBalance pic.twitter.com/KqBg6i0pMd
Por fortuna, los Dodgers se prepararon durante la temporada ante una eventual ausencia prolongada de su superestrella. Por esa razón, adquirieron al pitcher Tarik Skubal antes de la fecha límite de intercambios para fortalecer una rotación de lanzadores que buscará llegar en las mejores condiciones a la postemporada.
Shohei Ohtani could resume swinging Monday or Tuesday as he continues recovering from lingering right biceps and left knee issues.
Ohtani is eligible to return from the IL on September 23, giving him a short window to prepare for the postseason.#Dodgers #BlueDynasty pic.twitter.com/l2vdNja7kE
Además, los Dodgers llamó a uno de los mejores prospectos de las Grandes Ligas, Josue De Paula, para aportar a la ofensiva mientras Ohtani se recupera. El pelotero impresionó en sus primeros partidos ante los Marlins, una actuación que le permite a los Dodgers darle mayor tiempo de recuperación a Ohtani con la esperanza de que esté listo para disputar el Clásico de Otoño.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are one win away from clinching a National League playoff berth.
Monday, September 14, the Dodgers begin a three-game series against the Cincinnati Reds for the second time seven games.
Ahead of tonight’s game, the Dodgers make a couple changes in their lineup, one of them involving utility player Tommy Edman.
Tommy Edman is Back in the Lineup vs. the Reds After a Rest Day on Sunday
Per Los Angeles Dodgers reporter David Vassegh, the team announced their starting lineup against the Cincinnati Reds on Monday.
#Dodgers Lineup vs #Reds LHP, Nick Lodolo: Edman CF, Betts SS, Smith C, Tucker RF, T. Hernandez LF, Rojas 2B, Muncy 3B, E. Hernandez 1B, JDP DH, Tarik Skubal SP,” Vassegh wrote on X.
Edman sat out in Sunday’s loss against the Miami Marlins because Dodgers manager Dave Roberts, did not want him playing all three games on a turf field.
“#Dodgers Dave Roberts originally said Josue De Paula would DH all 3 games in Miami,” Dodgers insider Bill Plunket wrote on X ahead of Sunday’s game. “Thought it thru and decided he didn’t want Teoscar Hernandez or Tommy Edman to play all 3 games on turf here. So De Paula gets the start in LF.”
Edman and the Dodgers have been carefully monitoring the center fielder’s ankle, after spending nearly half the season on the injured list. The 31-year-old underwent an offseason ankle surgery and did not return to the Dodgers lineup until June 17.
While the Dodgers primary center fielder Andy Pages, remains on the injured list, Edman has spent most of starts in center.
Despite slashing .257/.339/.390 in 72 games, Edman’s seven game stretch shows signs of a quite the slump.
He’s batting .091 with five strikeouts, two hits, and two RBIs in his last 22 at-bats. Both of hits coming against the Washington Nationals on September 6.
Hopefully yesterday’s much needed rest day gets Edman back where he needs to be.
Los Angeles Dodgers Magic Number to Win NL West is Four
There only 15 days until the first MLB postseason game, and 13 games left in the season for the Dodgers. They can clinch a postseason berth tonight with a win against the Reds.
“LAD can clinch a postseason berth today with a win at Cincinnati *or* losses by both the Padres (@ COL) AND the Diamondbacks (v. MIA),” Dodgers beat writer Katie Woo wrote on X.
For the National League West, the Dodgers’ magic number is four.
After their series concludes against the Reds, the Dodgers are strictly facing NL West opponents. Two series at-home against the San Francisco Giants and San Diego Padres, and rounding off the season on the road to face San Francisco for the final time in 2026.

item.content:encoded:
El jardinero de 21 años abandonó Nueva York durante la pandemia para intentar firmar como profesional en República Dominicana. Los Dodgers lo contrataron por US$397,500 y cuatro años después se saltó Triple-A para llegar a Grandes Ligas.
El primer hit de Josué De Paula en las Grandes Ligas no fue un sencillo para guardar discretamente en una vitrina. Fue un cuadrangular de tres carreras.
El domingo, en Miami, el joven jardinero de los Dodgers encontró una recta de Eury Pérez y la envió al segundo nivel del jardín derecho del loanDepot park. La pelota recorrió unos 416 pies y salió del bate a 108.2 millas por hora. Más tarde agregó un doble y terminó de 2-2 en la derrota 6-4 de Los Ángeles ante los Marlins.
Era apenas su tercer día como jugador de Grandes Ligas.
La imagen resume una historia que comenzó de manera poco convencional. De Paula nació el 24 de mayo de 2005 en Brooklyn, Nueva York. Creció en Estados Unidos, asistió a Benjamin N. Cardozo High School, en Queens, y pertenece a una familia con antecedentes deportivos: es primo segundo de los exjugadores de la NBA Stephon Marbury y Sebastian Telfair.
Pero su camino hacia el béisbol profesional no pasó inicialmente por el sistema estadounidense de escuelas secundarias, universidades y draft.
Pasó por República Dominicana.
La pandemia cambió el camino
De Paula apenas había disputado su primer partido de béisbol con Cardozo cuando la pandemia de COVID-19 paralizó el deporte escolar en 2020.
Durante ese período, según relató posteriormente el propio jugador, su padre le planteó una alternativa: trasladarse a República Dominicana y tratar de abrirse paso por la ruta que cada año siguen cientos de prospectos latinoamericanos que entrenan para conseguir contratos con organizaciones de Grandes Ligas.
La familia se trasladó al país en 2021. De Paula tenía 15 años.
En Santo Domingo entrenó en El Niche Baseball Academy. El cambio era considerable: había nacido y crecido en Nueva York, pero entraba ahora al competitivo sistema dominicano de desarrollo de prospectos internacionales.
La apuesta tardó apenas unos meses en producir resultados.
US$397,500 y una firma que terminó pareciendo barata
El 15 de enero de 2022, cuando tenía 16 años, De Paula firmó con los Dodgers como agente libre internacional por un bono de US$397,500. Aunque nació en Estados Unidos, fue captado y firmado desde República Dominicana.
No era el nombre principal de aquella clase internacional de Los Ángeles. Los Dodgers anunciaron alrededor de 30 firmas y la atención se concentraba entonces sobre todo en otros prospectos de mayor cotización.
Con el tiempo, esos US$397,500 comenzaron a parecer una inversión muy favorable para la organización.
Su primera prueba profesional ocurrió precisamente en el país donde había buscado la firma.
En 2022 jugó para DSL Dodgers Bautista en la Dominican Summer League. Bateó .349, tuvo porcentaje de embazarse de .448 y slugging de .522 en 53 partidos, con cinco jonrones, 30 carreras impulsadas, 42 anotadas y 16 bases robadas. Fue seleccionado al equipo Todos Estrellas de postemporada de la liga.
El experimento dominicano había funcionado.
El difícil salto a Estados Unidos
En 2023 comenzó el recorrido por el sistema de ligas menores de Estados Unidos con Rancho Cucamonga, sucursal Clase A de los Dodgers.
Allí apareció una de las características que después llamaría la atención de la organización: su capacidad de controlar la zona de strike. En 74 partidos bateó .284, llegó a base a ritmo de .396 y produjo 40 carreras. El poder, sin embargo, todavía no había llegado: solo conectó dos cuadrangulares.
El crecimiento se hizo más evidente en 2024.
Entre Rancho Cucamonga y Great Lakes jugó 107 encuentros y terminó con promedio de .268, OBP de .404, 10 jonrones, 62 remolcadas y 27 bases robadas. Además negoció 84 transferencias, una cifra que reflejaba su disciplina en el plato a una edad en la que muchos prospectos todavía dependen casi exclusivamente de sus condiciones físicas.
Durante una de esas temporadas muertas entrenó en Miami junto a Juan Soto y Elly De La Cruz. La atención comenzó a trasladarse hacia el desarrollo de poder en un cuerpo de 6 pies y 3 pulgadas.
Los Dodgers empezaron a hablar de él en términos poco habituales. Dentro de la organización llegó a ser considerado uno de los bateadores jóvenes más avanzados desarrollados por el club en años recientes.
El jonrón que lo puso delante de todos
La explosión mediática llegó en julio.
De Paula fue seleccionado para el Juego de Futuras Estrellas y encontró a dos corredores en circulación frente al zurdo Noah Schultz, otro de los principales prospectos de MLB.
Conectó un slider y mandó la pelota 416 pies por el jardín derecho-central. El batazo salió a 108.5 millas por hora, dio ventaja 3-2 a la Liga Nacional y terminó convirtiéndolo en el Jugador Más Valioso del partido.
Era el primer prospecto de los Dodgers que recibía ese reconocimiento desde Chin-Lung Hu en 2007. Entre los dominicanos que lo habían ganado anteriormente estaban Alfonso Soriano y José Reyes.
Su temporada terminó con 12 cuadrangulares y 32 robos. Tras 98 encuentros con Great Lakes recibió finalmente el ascenso a Doble-A Tulsa, pero allí tuvo un aterrizaje abrupto: se fue sin hits en 18 turnos durante cuatro partidos.
Fue una pausa, no un techo.
¿Jugó con el Escogido?
De Paula pertenece a los Leones del Escogido.
El equipo lo seleccionó en la tercera ronda del Sorteo de Novatos de Lidom de 2023, cuando todavía era un jugador de Clase A de los Dodgers.
Sin embargo, en las fuentes oficiales y registros revisados no aparece evidencia de que haya disputado hasta ahora un partido oficial de temporada regular con los Leones. Es decir, sus derechos en el béisbol otoño-invernal dominicano pertenecen al Escogido, pero su desarrollo competitivo se ha mantenido dentro del sistema de los Dodgers.
El año que abrió la puerta
En 2026 regresó a Tulsa y convirtió Doble-A en su plataforma de lanzamiento.
En 124 partidos bateó .303, con .401 de porcentaje de embasarse y .547 de slugging. Disparó 27 jonrones, produjo 104 carreras y robó 31 bases. En toda su trayectoria de ligas menores acumuló 460 partidos con línea ofensiva de .286/.404/.453, 56 cuadrangulares y 280 impulsadas.
Ascenso a Grandes Ligas
También mejoró una variable que suele determinar si un bateador joven puede trasladar su producción a las Mayores: redujo su porcentaje de ponches mientras aumentaba considerablemente el poder.
En los entrenamientos de primavera ya había dado señales. Bateó .375 en 14 encuentros y volvió a participar en el Juego de Futuras Estrellas durante el verano.
Todavía faltaba un escalón: Triple-A.
Los Dodgers decidieron saltárselo.
De Doble-A directamente a sustituir a Ohtani
La oportunidad apareció cuando Los Ángeles colocó a Shohei Ohtani en la lista de lesionados.
El 11 de septiembre, los Dodgers seleccionaron el contrato de De Paula desde Tulsa. Para incorporarlo al roster de 40 jugadores trasladaron al lanzador Eric Lauer a la lista de lesionados de 60 días.
El movimiento resultó especialmente significativo: De Paula se convirtió en el primer jugador de posición de los Dodgers en saltar directamente de Doble-A a Grandes Ligas en más de una década.
Ni siquiera él esperaba que ocurriera de esa manera.
Cuando el dirigente de Tulsa, Eric Wedge, lo llamó a su oficina y le informó que tomaría un avión para reunirse con "los muchachos grandes", De Paula contó que inicialmente no entendió hacia dónde lo estaban enviando. Pensaba que Triple-A era el paso siguiente.
El viernes 11 de septiembre apareció como bateador designado y séptimo en la alineación contra Miami. Tenía 21 años y 110 días, convirtiéndose en uno de los Dodgers más jóvenes en debutar durante los últimos años. No consiguió hit en tres turnos, pero recibió una transferencia.
Dos días después ocupó por primera vez los jardines.
Y entonces llegó Eury Pérez.
De Paula conectó su primer hit de Grandes Ligas, un jonrón de tres carreras, y luego agregó un doble. Cuatro años y ocho meses después de firmar por US$397,500 en República Dominicana, el muchacho que salió de Brooklyn durante una pandemia y volvió al Caribe buscando una oportunidad ya estaba produciendo carreras para los Dodgers en septiembre.
La lesión de Ohtani abrió la puerta. Sus cuatro años atravesando la Dominican Summer League, Clase A, Clase A Avanzada y Doble-A explican por qué los Dodgers decidieron que no necesitaba tocar ninguna otra antes de entrar.

MIAMI –– The Dodgers’ bullpen melted down once again on Sunday in Miami.
Only this time, they got an unhelpful hand from some shaky late-game defense.
In a 6-4 loss to the Miami Marlins, the Dodgers allowed all of the scoring in the final two innings of what became a walk-off defeat; watching three high-leverage relievers –– Edgardo Henriquez, Tanner Scott and Brock Stewart –– falter after their infield gave away extra outs behind them.
In Henriquez’s two-run eighth inning, one would-be groundout instead snuck between shortstop Mookie Betts and second baseman Miguel Rojas, leaving Rojas injured after he made a late sliding attempt. Another got stuck in Betts’ hand while he tried to make a charging throw on the run, gifting the Marlins a free scoring opportunity that would lead to a two-run single from Otto Lopez.
The four-run ninth inning, which was capped off by Agustín Ramírez’s walk-off homer against Stewart, was just as frustrating, as Scott’s bid for a four-out save imploded after a pair of infield singles; one on a bunt, and another on a bad underhand flipped from a hobbled Freddie Freeman at first base.
“When you give a team extra outs,” manager Dave Roberts said, “that’s what happens.”
Initially, it appeared as though the Dodgers might still escape.
After Lopez’s single in the eighth, Scott replaced Henriquez to face Griffin Conine and struck him out on three pitches to end the inning and keep a 3-2 lead intact.
In the top of the ninth, the Dodgers added to the advantage on Betts’ RBI double, giving them “enough to win” offensively, as Roberts put it, even though they left the bases loaded later in the frame.
Alas, the bottom of the ninth immediately went sideways on an Xavier Edwards ground ball to lead off the inning.
Freeman, who has been playing through a knee injury and is mired in a 1-for-26 slump, fielded the ball but made a bad underhand flip back to first. Scott had to adjust to it as he went to cover the base, and was too late to recover as Edwards beat the play out.
Jakob Marsee came up next and executed a perfect bunt inside the third-base line.
Then, Javier Sanoja got jammed by a slider but still muscled a two-run double into the left-field corner.
Just like that, the Dodgers’ lead was gone. It was only Scott’s fourth blown save in 26 opportunities this season, but also the sixth time in his last 11 outings he has given up a run.
“Actually, I think the last week has been really good as far as the stuff,” Roberts said when asked of that trend, which has pushed Scott’s ERA to 2.91. “Today I think was just an odd day.”
Four pitches later, the game was over. Stewart came in to face the pinch-hitting Ramírez, but grooved him a fastball that was launched to left for the walk-off blast.
“It was supposed to be up above the zone. That’s where my fastball plays best,” Stewart said. “Just missed my spot, threw it right down the middle.”
Thus, the Dodgers suffered a loss that wasted big days from Emmet Sheehan (who threw six scoreless innings in his start) and Josue De Paula (who mashed a monstrous three-run home run in the fourth inning for his first career hit), while also delaying any possibility of clinching a playoff spot for a second-straight day.
“It’s baseball,” Roberts said. “It sucks. It feels bad. But that’s part of the thing.”
With a sigh, he later added: “But yeah, today was a crappy one.”
